Title: "Fun and VTES (was Re: some other thread somewhere)

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Andrew wrote:
>>Sure it can. In a practical test, when players flip the bird and
storm off in a rage, this is scored in the "not fun" column.>>

This means that *they* are not having fun. It doesn't mean that *others* are
not having fun. Thus, the quotient of fun being had is undefinable. Are we to
plan our actions, decks, and strategies around what the pissed off guy
considers fun? Then others are doubtlessly not going to have fun.

>>When players stick around until the end and there is general merriment, this
is scored in the "fun" column.>>

In the game used as example (dude flipping me the bird and leaving the table in
disgust), the other 4 players stuck around until the end of the game and there
was general merriment. Does this mean that my Rush deck suddenly became fun
simply because this guy got up and left? Was it not fun all along, but the
other three people at the table were incapable of knowing this?

>>If observation is not enough, you can just ask people, "are we having fun
yet?".>>

And if half of them answer "yes" and half of them answer "no" what have you
proven? What if 80% of them answer "yes" and 20% answer "no"? Or the other way
around? What does this prove?

>>You may get different answers from different people but this is no surprise
and no reason not to ask the question.>>

Certainly no reason to no ask the question, but expecting it to mean anything
is silly.

"Fun" is an undefinable concept, when applied to a group as a whole. Some
people like watching American Football. They love it to death. Me? I find it
unbearably boring. I'm not, on the other hand, going to tell these people to
stop watching Footbal, simply becasue *I* don't like it.

In a game like VTES,there is no way to define and enforce what is or is not
"fun" play. You can enforce the rules (as they are concretely defined), but
without developing quantifiable rules that define "fun" play, you can't enforce
such an idea. Trying to come up with a set of "fun" rules is doubtlessly going
to fail, as it will be fun for some folks and not fun for others. And saying
"just play for fun, and it will be fun" gets you nowhere, as person A's idea of
"fun" is probably wildly different than person B's idea of "fun". Personally, I
think it is fun when I sit at a table with a group of players who are all
trying to win and playing hardcore decks that can win--that deck that won the
German championship? I like decks like that. I like playing in games with
weenie bleed Dom hordes, Misdirection or no. I like playing in games with decks
like that. I like when my opponents play decks like that. It makes me happy. I
think Rush decks are fun. Thus, we have (at minimum) two wildly different views
of what "fun" is, and any attempt at a quantifiable defenition of "fun" falls
flat.

When that guy flipped me the bird and stormed off in disgust? I was having fun
(up until that particular point...). He was not. Who was right?

Nope, I'm pretty sure we could come up with a "fun-ness score". What
you would do is take all the cards in your deck, divide it into 23 even
piles (if your deck doesn't divide into 23 even piles, it isn't a fun
deck) turn over the top card on each, and if any match, you must pull
all but one copy from the face-up cards, writing down the number of
cards you removed as a negative score, and replace them with an equal
number of cards, none of which are the same card (by title). Now, you
add up the number of cards in your deck, adjust for the negative rating
(if any) you acquired in the previous step. Now, flip each pile over
and repeat. If (in either of these steps) none of the cards matched,
you get +10 fun.

Now that you have checked both ends of your stacks, shuffle all the
cards together. Draw 7 cards. If any of these are the same card, you
get -6 fun. If they are all different, you get +3 fun. Shuffle the
cards again. Sort the cards into 7 equal piles (again, if it doesn't
divide evenly, your deck is not fun, and you must start over). Pick
card x from pile x (card 1 from pile 1, card 2 from pile 2, etc.), and
if they are all different, you get +15 fun. If two are the same, you
only get +5 fun. If 3 are the same, you get +0 fun. 4 or more, -20
fun.

Finally, your fun score is decremented by 1 for each object you are
pelted with during a game in which the deck is played. If anyone
laughs at one of your merry japes during play, you get +1 fun.

> When that guy flipped me the bird and stormed off in disgust? I was
> having fun (up until that particular point...). He was not. Who was
> right?

Anyone that forgets this is a game and gets that upset over it is just
wrong in the head. I can understand getting annoyed if someone is
playing poorly, making really awful decisions, but that's not really
any reason to get extra-pissy. I have taken to warning people once
that I think they're making a bad decision (politely, in an even tone),
and if they persist, I just shut the hell up and figure that they'll
learn eventually. (Even when I'm back-ousted.) Social pressure to
play well will eventually catch up with them. If they're eternally a
poor player because they just suck, it's not my problem...

Of course, I still love your anecdote, Peter. Getting flipped off for
playing a rush deck rules. I think it's possibly even better than
sweeping. I've gotten a sweep here and there, but I've never gotten
the finger...you're still my hero, Peter. :)

Xian

I'll take a stab at it...I don't think there's really any question that
the predator of the quitter (or whatever...poor sport...) should get
the VP or the 6 pool...I think it's a matter of when.

In a tournament situation, if the player actually got up and left, I'd
be inclined to call it an example of Unsportsmanlike Conduct (Major)
and penalize with a Game Loss (and a Warning, as specified in the
penalty guidelines). I don't think it would quite require a
Disqualification, but I'd be up for it if the person was really acting
up. :) Thus, I'd probably give the person the VP & pool there and
then. Or, I'd resolve it with the resolution I'd use in a firendly
game, which would be...

Have the predator bleed through the remaining pool as if there were no
minions to block or deflect, etc. Once that static amount of pool is
removed, the predator gains the VP & pool. This is probably the best
way to handle it.

Hmmm. So let me see if I understand the argument correctly: It's unfair
to make a combat deck bleed his dropped-out prey to get his VPs and his pool
reward because this would approximate a prey who sacrificed his chance of
winning the game (by not spending his pool on minions he'd need to oust _his_
prey) to screw over his predator? Closing the loop on some of your
arguments (and correct me if I've some missed a vital point), this seems
to be the gist of it.

If so, you have kind of a minor point, I suppose. I'm not too disturbed
by it, though, because there's so much screwiness in what players choose
to do by chance that I suspect this is almost noise. People create
mad intercept decks full of superior Obedience that are an absolute
torch for their predators and a skate for their prey (as long as their
prey concentrates on bleeding). Rush decks in general are a rip-off for
their neighbors on either side and a boon to their grandpredators and
grandprey. Having a predator who does stealth/bleed is awfully
tough (unless you're a combat deck) because even if you can outrace him
to that victory point, you're still limping - but it's great for your
grandpredator if you can manage to slow him down. The grandpredator
has a decent chance of ousting you both relatively easily.

> If the player who walks out has little pool, then it's not a problem, and I
> agree that it's best to allow him to bleed unopposed until his prey
> 'properly' dies.

I actually would expect his rule to get used more in mid/late game.
In the early game, just start the thing over.

If it happens in a tournament, the judge should make whatever
arrangements (regarding pool, VPs, cards in play, etc.) he
determines are necessary to best preserve the game state for
the remaining players.

If it happens in a "friendly" game, it might be time to
evaluate the definition of friendly. :-)

Then again, I had a JOL game where my prey decided to stop doing anything (he
would just answer "no block" or post a "done" message as his turn, with any
actions needed by other cards on the table). Both his vamps (big ones) were in
torpor, and he had 10 or 11 pool left when he decided to become a wall.

It was VERY frustrating. I had a bruise and bleed deck, heavy on the bruising,
light on the bleeding. I fell to my Setite predator before I could oust my
prey.

>around till the job is finished), but when they still have enough pool to

>stuck around hoping that my predator got ousted while I still have enough
>pool to get a few vamps out and get back in the game. The best way to
>frustrate a combat deck is to give him no targets.

Nah, that guy had no chance of making it even with my own oust. We were three
bleeders all waiting to get a shot at him.

>If the player who walks out has little pool, then it's not a problem, and I
>agree that it's best to allow him to bleed unopposed until his prey
>'properly' dies.

Logically, the meth who leaves the table like that should be declared a Bad
Loser, and his predator should get the VP and pool, immediatly.
However, this might bring about a new type of play into the game. The strategy
of "Pissing your prey", i.e. doing everything you can to properly and
thoroughly angering your prey until he quits the game. We must NOT go there.

Man, if we allow that strategy, the world of Jyhad will tremble whenever my
name is pronounced, for I am quite an annoying little bugger. And I can do it
quite legally too. It would be very hard to pinpoint anything in the floor
rules to forbid my actions.
